analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare hospitals to set nurse staffing plans and publish daily nurse levels.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced by one senator with no cosponsors, sent to the Senate Finance Committee, and never received a hearing, vote, or further action before the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made Medicare participation conditional on hospitals creating a written staffing plan for nurses. Each hospital would need a staffing committee made mostly of direct-care nurses, adjustable minimum nurse-to-patient ratios for each unit and shift, daily public posting of nurse staffing numbers, federal reporting of nurse-sensitive quality data, civil fines for violations, whistleblower protection for staff, and the right for a nurse to refuse an assignment that violates the plan or her training. The idea behind it, stated in the bill's own findings, is that thin nurse staffing leads to more medication errors, patient deaths, readmissions, and nurse burnout.
analysis.who_benefits: Hospital patients, who get more nurses per patient and public staffing data to compare hospitals; and nurses, who get enforceable staffing floors, protection from retaliation for complaining, and the right to refuse unsafe assignments.

how_it_helps.text: Every Medicare hospital would have to implement a hospital-wide nurse staffing plan built on adjustable minimum registered-nurse-to-patient ratios for each unit and each shift, with no state staffing law weakened and no minimum usable as a ceiling [S3].
A staffing committee in each hospital, at least 55% of whose members are direct-care registered nurses rather than managers or administrators, would write, monitor, and update the plan annually [S3].

Hospitals would have to post daily, in a visible place, the number of licensed and unlicensed nursing staff on each unit and shift, and the Secretary would publish the data on the Hospital Compare website so patients can compare hospitals [S3].

Nurses could refuse assignments that violate the staffing plan or that they are not trained for, and hospitals could not retaliate against employees or patients who file staffing complaints; prevailing employees could win reinstatement and back pay, and prevailing patients $5,000 in added damages [S3].

The bill's findings cite research that better staffing reduces readmissions Medicare pays nothing for, and that turnover costs the average hospital nearly $5 million a year, arguing staffing improvements largely pay for themselves [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals, which would bear the cost of hiring more registered nurses, running staffing committees, posting and reporting data, and potential fines of up to $10,000 per knowing violation (with higher penalties for repeat violators); costs could flow through to insurers and patients in hospital prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Hospitals, through hiring and compliance costs

drawbacks.text: The bill does not impose fixed national ratios; it lets each hospital's own committee set 'upwardly adjustable minimums,' and the main penalty for violations starts at no more than $10,000 per violation — a modest sum for a hospital — so enforcement could be weak in practice [S3].

Hospitals would face real compliance costs: hiring additional registered nurses in a tight labor market, committee operations, daily posting, and federal data reporting, with only two years (four for rural hospitals) to implement [S3].

An honest supporter would acknowledge that some of the cost could surface as higher hospital prices or tighter admission decisions, and that the bill excludes emergency exemptions narrowly, which hospitals would argue could strain surge capacity despite the declared-emergency carve-out [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is concrete and well-documented in the bill's own findings: fewer medication errors, deaths, readmissions, and nurse burnout. The design is deliberately flexible rather than a rigid federal ratio, which reduces the risk of unintended staffing distortions but also weakens the guarantee. The main honest cost is hospital compliance spending, much of which the cited research suggests is offset by lower turnover and readmission penalties. On balance a moderate, targeted mandate with real but imperfect teeth.

outcome.mechanism: It went straight to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced and sat there until the Congress ended, with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote.

narrative.text: Senator Jeff Merkley introduced the Safe Staffing for Nurse and Patient Safety Act of 2018 on February 15, 2018 [S1][S5].
The bill's only actions were introduction and referral to the Senate Committee on Finance, which took no further action on it before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals avoided a federal staffing mandate, public daily staffing disclosure, and fines; patients and nurses got none of the bill's protections.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hospitals that avoided a staffing mandate

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Senate Finance Committee; no other senator joined.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day of introduction and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

against.name: Hospital industry
against.what_they_did: Hospital associations have opposed federal mandatory nurse staffing requirements as inflexible and costly, and the industry had a strong financial stake in the bill's failure.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred and no other senator cosponsored, so the partisan shape of the issue was never tested; the bill died from inaction rather than opposition votes.

industries.note: Hospitals would have had to hire more registered nurses, operate nurse-majority staffing committees, post daily staffing levels publicly, report quality data, and face fines. Hospitals currently control staffing levels with limited public disclosure, and thin staffing is a direct cost saving for them, so their financial interest ran against the bill's patient-safety purpose.
Nurses would gain enforceable staffing floors, protection from retaliation, and the right to refuse unsafe assignments, which overlaps directly with patient safety.
